title: Carboplatin + fluorouracil after nasopharyngeal chemoradiotherapy
context_label: Adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced stage III or IV nasopharyngeal cancer when cisplatin cannot be used or tolerated.
indication_text: Adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced stage III or IV nasopharyngeal cancer when cisplatin cannot be used or tolerated.
purpose: This chemotherapy is an additional treatment after chemoradiotherapy for nasopharyngeal cancer. It aims to treat cancer cells that may remain. The team explains the expected benefit and burden for you, including recovery from the earlier treatment.
schedule_label: Every 28 days, for up to 3 cycles after chemoradiotherapy.
schedule_summary: After recovery, adjuvant chemotherapy is planned to begin 4 weeks after completion of weekly carboplatin with radiotherapy (NCCP 00419). Carboplatin is given on Day 1 and fluorouracil over Days 1–4, every 28 days for up to 3 cycles. The treating team confirms readiness and dates.
administration_text: Carboplatin is infused over 30 minutes on Day 1. Its dose is calculated from kidney function using a target exposure called AUC 5. Fluorouracil 1,000 mg/m² per day is given as a continuous 96-hour infusion, or as the source-listed daily 22-hour option on Days 1–4. Your unit confirms the actual prescription, pump changes and disconnection time.
monitoring_summary: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests before each cycle. Review mouth soreness, swallowing, weight, intake and painful palms or soles; hearing and nerve symptoms also need review. If kidney function changes, the carboplatin calculation may need reassessment.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin.
agents.watch: Report fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.mechanism: Disrupts production of DNA and RNA
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
agents.watch: Report severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection
Rare severe neurological or early excessive toxicity

monitoring_schedule.note: Required regimen tests, symptom-triggered investigations and cancer-response tests serve different purposes. Ask who books each test and who explains the result.

monitoring_test_details.label: Full blood count
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Checks infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline and before each cycle

monitoring_test_details.label: Kidney and liver tests
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Guide safe treatment and identify organ problems.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline and before each cycle

monitoring_test_details.label: DPD assessment
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Checks for reduced ability to break down fluorouracil; results affect treatment choice or dose. Testing cannot exclude every severe reaction. Kidney impairment can affect one blood-based test, so the team chooses the appropriate method.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Before the first fluorouracil treatment unless already tested

monitoring_test_details.label: Kidney filtration assessment
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Carboplatin dose is calculated from kidney filtration. A measured test is preferred where feasible; the team chooses a valid method and reassesses significant changes.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Before treatment; reassessment when kidney function or the clinical situation changes

monitoring_test_details.label: Hearing assessment
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Investigates hearing loss or tinnitus and helps judge platinum-related risk.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline when clinically indicated; review new hearing or balance symptoms during treatment

monitoring_test_details.label: Imaging and tumour-specific tests
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Assesses the cancer rather than whether a treatment-day blood count is safe.
monitoring_test_details.timing: As individually arranged for the disease and symptoms; no universal marker panel or imaging interval

Kidney results guide carboplatin dosing. Report reduced urine, persistent vomiting or dehydration.

Report sore, red or peeling palms or soles before they limit walking or ordinary activities.
Report tinnitus, hearing change, numbness or tingling, especially after earlier platinum treatment.
Fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding needs prompt oncology advice.
Tell staff about pain, redness or swelling at the line, or itching, wheeze or faintness during infusion.

support.title: One written support-medicine plan
support.text: Ask for one list separating prevention medicines, rescue treatment and regular medicines. The schedule must match this treatment and visit. Record what you take and whether it helps; do not double a dose, restart an old prescription or add medicines without checking.

support.title: Preventing sickness
support.text: This platinum-containing combination needs an agreed anti-sickness plan. Take prevention medicines at the stated times and keep rescue instructions available. Contact the team for persistent vomiting or inability to drink.

support.title: Food, fluids and weight
support.text: Tell the team early about reduced intake or weight loss. A dietitian can adapt food texture, supplements and intake goals. Follow an individual fluid plan, especially with kidney or heart problems.

support.title: Mouth and swallowing care
support.text: Follow the mouth-care and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, thrush or swallowing difficulty early. Ask for a swallowing assessment if food or drinks make you cough or choke; do not assume a general food texture is safe for you.

support.title: Fertility, pregnancy and medicine checks
support.text: Before treatment, discuss fertility, contraception, pregnancy and breastfeeding, including medicine-specific precautions after treatment. Bring all prescription, over-the-counter and herbal medicines to review. The team must check interactions and allergies.

sections.title: Before the first visit
sections.text: Bring your medicines and allergy list, test dates, treatment calendar and actual emergency contacts. Tell the unit about swallowing, hearing, mobility, transport or communication needs.

sections.title: Time in the unit

Your unit confirms the actual prescription, pump changes and disconnection time.

sections.title: Infusion and appointment planning
sections.text: Continuous fluorouracil over 96 hours, or the prescribed daily 22-hour option on Days 1–4; confirm actual pump visits.

sections.title: Before you leave
sections.text: Check the next treatment and test dates, medicines, pump or line appointments, and who to contact if unwell. Have the team replace and verify every example phone number on the wallet card.

sections.title: Practical support
sections.text: Ask about transport, work, costs, caring responsibilities, an interpreter or a support person. Keep changes to the plan in one record.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis
chapters.intro: Keep the pathology, stage and agreed treatment aim with your records.

items.title: Site and type
items.text: Nasopharyngeal cancer starts in the upper throat behind the nose. The team explains stage, biopsy findings and any Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) testing relevant to your cancer.

items.title: Who this plan is for
items.text: Adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced stage III or IV nasopharyngeal cancer when cisplatin cannot be used or tolerated.

items.title: Cancer tests and treatment-safety tests
items.text: A scan or a tumour-specific test assesses the cancer. Blood counts and kidney or liver tests assess treatment safety. DPD testing concerns fluorouracil metabolism and is not a measure of cancer response.

chapters.title: Treatment choices and your priorities
chapters.intro: The consent discussion sets out the personal aim and boundaries.

items.title: Expected benefit and alternatives
items.text: This chemotherapy is an additional treatment after chemoradiotherapy for nasopharyngeal cancer. It aims to treat cancer cells that may remain. The team explains the expected benefit and burden for you, including recovery from the earlier treatment. Ask about reasonable alternatives, including supportive care, and which outcomes matter most to you. A research result cannot predict an individual outcome.

items.title: Changing or stopping treatment
items.text: The team may delay, reduce, omit or stop a medicine after symptoms or test results, a change in benefit or your preference. Record which medicine is affected and what is required before restarting. Do not use an old prescription to restart treatment.

items.title: Other treatment and off-label use
items.text: NCCP identifies carboplatin in this nasopharyngeal indication as an off-label use. Discuss why it is being offered, the evidence, alternatives and uncertainties, and document consent under local policy. The earlier carboplatin-radiotherapy course is a separate completed stage. This adjuvant course begins only after recovery and confirmation of the next plan.

chapters.title: Preparing for your treatment visits
chapters.intro: Use the medicine schedule and logistics pages for the exact visit pattern.

items.title: Your personal checklist
items.text: Check that the treatment name, planned tests, support medicines, transport and urgent contacts are correct. Explain any previous infusion reaction or change in your health before the medicine is prepared.

items.title: When dates change
items.text: A missed or held dose is not a completed dose. Ask for revised blood-test, treatment and pump dates where relevant. The team must clarify whether an omitted weekly dose changes later dates.

items.title: Recording actual treatment
items.text: Record the actual date and medicines received, dose changes, test results and symptoms. The wallet is a brief portable record; the passport holds more detail and does not replace hospital records.

chapters.title: Between visits: symptoms and home medicines
chapters.intro: Symptoms do not follow a guaranteed calendar.

items.title: Responding early
items.text: Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, or unusually early severe symptoms, needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency.

items.title: One usable medicine list
items.text: Keep prevention, rescue and regular medicines separately labelled. Note doses actually taken and whether symptoms improve. Check new prescription, over-the-counter and herbal medicines with the team; do not add or repeat old courses without advice.

items.title: Nerve symptoms and daily function
items.text: Report numbness, tingling, weakness, falls, difficulty doing buttons or changes in walking. Describe what you can no longer do, not just a symptom score. The team may need to change treatment before symptoms worsen.

chapters.title: Mouth, teeth and jaw care
chapters.intro: This is the home for detailed mouth and dental advice.

items.title: Care during chemotherapy
items.text: Use the prescribed gentle oral-care and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, infection, bleeding or pain that affects eating or drinking. Check with oncology before dental procedures.

items.title: If you have had head and neck radiation
items.text: Earlier radiation can affect saliva, teeth, jaw movement and healing long after it ends. Tell your dentist about it before invasive treatment and continue the advised preventive care. Radiation-related recovery is relevant to this adjuvant plan.

chapters.title: Eating, drinking and maintaining strength
chapters.intro: Adapt the plan to what you can manage safely.

items.title: Weight and intake
items.text: Record changes in weight and what limits eating: soreness, taste change, dry mouth, nausea or fatigue may need different help. A dietitian can adapt meals, supplements or feeding support. Do not wait for substantial weight loss to ask for review.

items.title: When fluids or food are not enough
items.text: Contact the team for persistent vomiting, dizziness, much less urine, inability to drink or severe diarrhoea. Fluid goals depend on kidney and heart health. If a feeding tube is needed, ask for training, supplies and a clear problem-contact route.

chapters.title: Swallowing, voice and communication
chapters.intro: Protect safe swallowing and make communication easier.

items.title: When to seek assessment
items.text: Report coughing or choking with food or drinks, a wet voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. Ask for speech and language assessment; use only the textures and exercises recommended for you.

items.title: Communication support
items.text: Tell the team about hearing, speech or voice changes. Request written instructions, an interpreter, communication aids or help involving a support person when useful.

chapters.title: Daily life and personal priorities
chapters.intro: Use the support available around you.

items.title: Activity, rest and practical needs
items.text: Discuss the level of activity you can manage, work, travel and help at home. Ask for assessment if fatigue, pain, weakness or falls disrupt ordinary activities. Bring practical barriers to appointments into the discussion.

items.title: Fertility, intimacy and emotional wellbeing
items.text: Ask about fertility preservation before treatment and specific pregnancy, contraception and breastfeeding precautions. Tell the team about anxiety, body-image, sexual or relationship concerns; support can be tailored to your priorities.

items.title: Smoking and alcohol
items.text: Ask for help with smoking cessation and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth symptoms, medicines and recovery may affect what is appropriate for you.

chapters.title: Recovery, review and longer-term care
chapters.intro: Finishing scheduled doses and recovering are different milestones.

items.title: Symptoms and follow-up
items.text: Continue recovery and follow-up after chemoradiotherapy and chemotherapy, including mouth, dental, swallowing, nutritional, hearing or nerve problems. Examinations, scans and any tumour-specific tests follow the agreed nasopharyngeal cancer plan; this regimen does not prescribe a universal interval.

items.title: The next cancer assessment
items.text: Record who arranges examinations, scans and any tumour-specific tests, and who explains the results. A general reference calendar does not set an appointment or mean a scan is overdue.

items.title: Information for other clinicians
items.text: Keep the regimen name, last treatment date, current medicines and unresolved side effects available. Tell future clinicians about any earlier head and neck radiotherapy, platinum-related hearing or kidney problems, and significant infusion reactions.

chapters.title: Your records and additional help
chapters.intro: Essential information should remain usable on paper.

items.title: Passport and treatment card
items.text: Use the passport for the fuller record and the wallet card for the treatment name, contacts and actual completed cycles. Its QR opens this treatment’s information; it does not contain a personal medical record or update paper stamps.

items.title: Complete local contacts
items.text: Every example telephone number must be replaced and checked by the treating service before patient use. Add daytime, out-of-hours and backup contacts and keep them accessible to a support person.

items.title: Reading without a phone
items.text: Read the full handbook in its chapter sequence. The treatment, symptom, contact and practical information does not require scanning a QR or following a hyperlink. Add questions to the passport and bring it to review.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: The NCCP regimen brings together evidence and specialist guidance for this particular treatment setting.
evidence.population: Adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced stage III or IV nasopharyngeal cancer when cisplatin cannot be used or tolerated.
evidence.comparison: Your team compares the expected benefit and burdens with appropriate alternatives for your disease and health.
evidence.interpretation: Evidence for a whole chemoradiotherapy-and-adjuvant strategy cannot isolate the benefit of this adjuvant component. This carboplatin pathway is used when cisplatin is unsuitable; it should not inherit a survival figure from a different cancer setting. Population: Adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiotherapy for locally advanced stage III or IV nasopharyngeal cancer when cisplatin cannot be used or tolerated. Comparison: Your team compares the expected benefit and burdens with appropriate alternatives for your disease and health. Your previous treatment, current health and disease extent affect the decision. Group research outcomes do not predict an individual outcome.

consent_support: Discuss the individual aim, expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainties; common, serious and lasting effects; infusion reactions and infection; fertility and pregnancy; treatment burden; support medicines and urgent contacts. NCCP identifies carboplatin in this nasopharyngeal indication as an off-label use. Discuss why it is being offered, the evidence, alternatives and uncertainties, and document consent under local policy.

Ask your team to write down the individual aim and explain reasonable alternatives, their burdens and the uncertainties before you decide.

Have the team replace the example numbers with verified daytime, out-of-hours and backup contacts before using the card.

questions.q: How will we decide whether to continue, change or stop?
questions.a: Your team reviews symptoms, test results, treatment benefit and your priorities. Ask when cancer-response assessment is planned and what would lead to a change. A delay or omitted dose must be recorded and does not count as treatment received.

questions.q: What support can help me manage treatment?
questions.a: Ask for a written support-medicine plan and early help with mouth pain, eating, drinking, swallowing, skin or nerve symptoms. Tell the team about travel, work, caring and communication needs. Dietitian, speech and language, nursing and other support can be arranged according to your needs.
